outcome: The conjecture itself (divergent reciprocal sum implies arbitrarily long APs) remains fully open, including the 3-term case in full generality, but a bound closely tied to it moved: Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17995, submitted 28 Feb 2024) proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}) for k≥5, the first improvement to Gowers' 2001 bound in 23 years.
summary: The stated conjecture — that a divergent sum of reciprocals of a set of positive integers forces arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions in that set — remains completely open, and is not known even for a single fixed length beyond what earlier work (Bloom–Sisask 2020, predating the frozen revision) established for 3-term APs in a related but weaker density-type formulation. I read erdosproblems.com's page for this problem (#3, $5000 prize, last updated 4 April 2026), the current live Wikipedia article, and the Quanta Magazine piece on grad students' 2024 progress. No source claims the conjecture, or any additional case of it, has been settled since 26 January 2024. What did happen in the window is a genuine, non-trivial tightening of the general bound r_k(N) (largest subset of {1,...,N} avoiding a non-trivial k-term AP) for k≥5: Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17995, submitted 28 Feb 2024, published in a 2024/2025 journal outlet per MIT author pages) proved r_k(N) ≪ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}), improving on Gowers' 2001 bound and marking (per Quanta) the first advance on this specific bound in 23 years. Erdős himself noted that pushing r_k(N) down to N/((log N)(log log N)^2) would suffice to prove his arithmetic-progressions conjecture, so this is a bound-type event genuinely connected to the conjecture's proof strategy, not a case of the conjecture settled (no specific divergent-reciprocal-sum set was shown to contain long APs) and not a variant with a different hypothesis — it operates on exactly the general averaging/density machinery the conjecture's proof would need. I classify this as status 'progress' rather than 'partial': the bound moved for the general Szemerédi-type problem underlying the conjecture, but no particular instance or restricted class of the conjecture (as opposed to the underlying combinatorial bound) was resolved, so I did not treat it as a settled 'case' under §3.1. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this chain: the Leng-Sah-Sawhney paper is standard human mathematics (a consequence of quasipolynomial Gowers-norm inverse theorem bounds plus the Heath-Brown/Szemerédi/Green-Tao density-increment strategy), with no acknowledgement of AI tools found in the available text, and the erdosproblems.com page for this exact problem explicitly lists no AI-assisted developments as of its 4 April 2026 update. I also checked whether the broader 2024-2026 wave of AI-solved Erdős problems (reported by Quanta's August 2026 piece 'Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI', covering GPT-5.2, Gemini/Aletheia, Harmonic's Aristotle, and OpenAI's internal 'Astra' model) touched this problem or a directly connected Erdős problem; that article does not mention problem #3 or this conjecture, and the AI-solved problems named there (#333, #728, #1051, #1196, the unit distance problem) are unrelated to arithmetic progressions with divergent reciprocal sums. I disagree with nothing in the triage: its verdict of 'none' correctly found no AI angle, though it missed the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound improvement, which I flag as a genuine mathematical event even though it changes no AI-relevant conclusion.
competing_reading: One could argue the Leng-Sah-Sawhney bound is a 'related problem' (an r_k(N) bound, not literally the divergence-implies-APs statement) and therefore beside the question per §3.1, making the correct status 'open' with no_change_found true rather than 'progress'. I chose 'progress' because the bound is not a different problem with different hypotheses (a 'variant') but is explicitly, by Erdős's own remark, the exact quantitative route to proving this conjecture — tightening it is the recognized proof strategy for the conjecture itself, not an analogue of it. If a stricter reading of §3.1 is preferred, this record would become 'open' / no_change_found instead.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that r_k(N) ≪ N/((log N)(log log N)^2) for all k, or any direct argument establishing the conjecture (or a genuine fixed case of it, e.g. for a specific named divergent-reciprocal-sum set) rather than a further bound improvement, would settle whether this event counts as more than 'progress'.

events.what: Leng, Sah and Sawhney prove r_k(N) << N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) for k>=5, improving Gowers' 2001 bound on sets in {1,...,N} avoiding k-term APs

judgement.doubts: The bullet is a qualitative statement (divergent reciprocal sum implies arbitrarily long APs) and names no quantity; r_k(N) is the quantitative Szemeredi problem. Per the record, Erdos noted r_k(N) << N/((log N)(log log N)^2) would suffice, and the new bound N·exp(-(log log N)^{c_k}) is far from that threshold, so it settles no length k and no class of sets for this bullet. A reader who treats the r_k(N) density as this bullet's own quantity would code 'progress'; I judge it a bound on a different (stronger-hypothesis) question. The record's summary also calls Bloom–Sisask 2020 a 'weaker density-type formulation', but that is pre-snapshot and does not affect the code.
